## How to use this starter

This lab repeats the lecture workflow with a new outcome: weight loss.
The three function definitions run as supplied. Exercise chunks use
`eval=FALSE`; remove that option as you work through each question in order.
Complete the TODOs and explanations. Rendering an untouched starter is not
completion. Use the supplied normal scenarios and Welch's test for the core lab.

## Simulation project: evaluating a weight-loss intervention

Can we reliably estimate and detect the additional weight loss from a new
intervention, and do our confidence intervals have the advertised coverage?

The outcome is weight lost after 12 weeks, in kg: positive values mean weight
loss and negative values mean weight gain. The control population mean is 1 kg;
the intervention mean is 1 kg under the null and 3 kg under the alternative.
The true additional weight loss, `delta`, is therefore 0 or 2 kg. All means,
SDs, and distribution choices below are hypothetical teaching assumptions.

## The three functions used throughout the lab

```{r}
# One trial: y is weight lost after 12 weeks (kg).
# Control mean = 1; intervention mean = 1 + delta.
simulate_trial <- function(n_ctrl, n_trt, sd_ctrl, sd_trt, delta = 0) {
  data.frame(
    arm = rep(x = c("ctrl", "trt"), times = c(n_ctrl, n_trt)),
    y = c(rnorm(n = n_ctrl, mean = 1, sd = sd_ctrl),
          rnorm(n = n_trt, mean = 1 + delta, sd = sd_trt))
  )
}

# Analyse one trial. The core lab uses Welch's test (pooled = FALSE).
analyse_trial <- function(data, pooled = FALSE) {
  treatment <- data$y[data$arm == "trt"]
  control <- data$y[data$arm == "ctrl"]
  fit <- t.test(x = treatment, y = control, var.equal = pooled)
  c(est = mean(x = treatment) - mean(x = control),
    se = fit$stderr, p = fit$p.value,
    lo = fit$conf.int[1], hi = fit$conf.int[2])
}

# Repeat one design row B times, like run_scenario() in the lecture.
run_study <- function(s, B, pooled = FALSE) {
  out <- replicate(n = B, expr = {
    d <- simulate_trial(n_ctrl = s$n_ctrl, n_trt = s$n_trt,
                        sd_ctrl = s$sd_ctrl, sd_trt = s$sd_trt,
                        delta = s$delta)
    analyse_trial(data = d, pooled = pooled)
  })
  data.frame(s, replicate = seq_len(B),
             as.data.frame(t(out)), row.names = NULL)
}
```

| Function | Role in this lab |
|---|---|
| `simulate_trial()` | Generates one trial's patient outcomes |
| `analyse_trial()` | Returns `est`, `se`, `p`, `lo`, and `hi` for one trial |
| `run_study()` | Repeats generation and analysis for one scenario |
| `rnorm()`, `rep()`, `c()`, `data.frame()` | Draw outcomes, create arm labels, and assemble data |
| `t.test()`, `mean()` | Fit the two-sample test and calculate means or proportions |
| `replicate()`, `t()`, `as.data.frame()` | Repeat an expression and put trials into rows |
| `expand.grid()` | Creates every combination of the chosen scenario values |
| `nrow()`, `seq_len()`, `vector()` | Count rows, create indices, and prepare a results list |
| `set.seed()`, `runif()`, `identical()` | Reproduce a run and check the seed experiment |
| `do.call()`, `rbind()` | Combine the list of scenario results into one table |
| `head()`, `summary()`, `tapply()`, `table()`, `subset()` | Inspect and select data |
| `sd()`, `sqrt()`, `sum()`, `round()` | Calculate spread, MCSE, counts, and rounded values |
| `plot()`, `arrows()`, `abline()`, `pmax()`, `pmin()` | Plot rates and bounded Monte Carlo intervals |

`for` repeats code over design rows; `function` defines a reusable function.
`$` selects a column or named result, `[i, ]` selects a row, and `[[i]]`
selects an element of a list. `rep()` repeats values; `replicate()` reruns code.

and performance measures. Use independent normal outcomes, control mean 1 kg,
intervention mean `1 + delta` kg, and SDs 4 and 2 kg. Explain what evidence could
support these teaching assumptions in a real study. Define the true mean
difference and distinguish it from an estimate in one trial.

Build `design` below. Explain why `expand.grid()` creates four rows, identify
what changes and what stays fixed, and describe row 3 in words. Each row is a
scenario, not a patient or a simulated trial. Why is there a separate seed for
each scenario?

```{r, eval=FALSE}
design <- expand.grid(n_ctrl = c(10, 30), delta = c(0, 2))
design$n_trt <- 40
design$sd_ctrl <- 4
design$sd_trt <- 2
design$scenario <- seq_len(nrow(design))
design$seed <- 1400 + design$scenario
design
design[3, ]
```

## 5. Run all four design rows

Use `B = 1000` for each scenario. Trace one pass through the loop: choose a
design row, set its seed, run the scenario, and store the result. Explain how
`do.call()` and `rbind()` combine the results. How many rows should `all_results`
contain? Verify the number of trials per scenario. Insert an unrelated
`runif()` call before a scenario's `set.seed()` and check that its results stay
unchanged. Do not reset the seed within the trial repetitions.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
B <- 1000
results <- vector(mode = "list", length = nrow(design))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(design))) {
  set.seed(design$seed[i])
  results[[i]] <- run_study(s = design[i, ], B = B)
}
all_results <- do.call(what = rbind, args = results)
nrow(all_results)
table(all_results$scenario)
# TODO: use runif(), set.seed(), and identical() to check reproducibility.
```

## 6. Summarize estimation and testing performance

For every scenario, report bias, empirical SE, coverage, rejection rate, and
MCSE of the rejection rate. Trace the supplied summary loop for one scenario.
Explain why `mean()` of a TRUE/FALSE condition gives a proportion.
Add mean confidence-interval width to the summary. Which values describe the
method's performance, which describe sampling variability, and which describe
Monte Carlo uncertainty? Interpret rejection as type I error for `delta = 0`
and power for `delta = 2`.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
summaries <- vector(mode = "list", length = nrow(design))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(design))) {
  one <- all_results[all_results$scenario == design$scenario[i], ]
  truth <- design$delta[i]
  rejection <- mean(x = one$p < 0.05)
  summaries[[i]] <- data.frame(
    design[i, ], trials = nrow(one),
    bias = mean(x = one$est) - truth,
    empirical_se = sd(x = one$est),
    coverage = mean(x = one$lo <= truth & truth <= one$hi),
    rejection = rejection,
    mcse_rejection = sqrt(rejection * (1 - rejection) / nrow(one)))
}
performance <- do.call(what = rbind, args = summaries)
performance
# TODO: add mean_width = mean(one$hi - one$lo) inside data.frame().
# Explain how each measure answers the study question.
```

## 8. Use power for study planning

Use the `delta = 2` results to compare power for the two allocations. Report
rejections, trials, power, MCSE, and an approximate 95% Monte Carlo interval.
Do the results support at least 80% power? Distinguish power from coverage:
which event does each count? Explain why increasing `B` alone cannot rescue
a study with low power. State that the conclusions depend on the assumed
outcome distribution, independence, means, and SDs.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
power_results <- subset(x = performance, subset = delta == 2)
power_results$power <- power_results$rejection
power_results$rejected <- round(power_results$power * power_results$trials)
power_results$mc_lower <- pmax(0, power_results$power -
                                1.96 * power_results$mcse_rejection)
# TODO: add mc_upper using pmin(1, power + 1.96 * mcse_rejection).

```

## Optional extension: compare Welch and pooled tests

Repeat one scenario with `pooled = TRUE`. Start both runs at the same scenario
seed so they use the same generated datasets. Compare null rejection rates
before interpreting differences in power. The core lab requires only Welch.

```r
set.seed(design$seed[1])
welch_results <- run_study(s = design[1, ], B = 1000)
set.seed(design$seed[1])
pooled_results <- run_study(s = design[1, ], B = 1000, pooled = TRUE)
```
